title: Senior's toolkit: debugging DNS
summary: dig with the flags that matter, asking a specific server, tracing delegation, and seeing what the local resolver and the app really get.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: debugging DNS
steps.body: "It's always DNS" is a joke because it is often true. The skill is asking the right server the right question, and comparing that with what the machine's resolver hands to the app.

toolkit.what: Just the answer: the addresses, or the CNAME chain and then the addresses. The first check after every DNS change.
flags: the answer section with TTLs, without the rest

toolkit.what: Asks one specific server instead of the system resolver. Comparing a public resolver, the corporate one and the authoritative one shows who still has the old answer.
flags: "answer from what you hold": against an authoritative server, shows what it really serves
use TCP (large answers, or UDP blocked)
toolkit.when: after a record change: is it published, or only cached somewhere?

toolkit.what: Walks the delegation from the root, to the TLD, to the domain's name servers, as a resolver would. Finds broken delegations and wrong NS records.
flags: follow referrals from the root, ignore caches

toolkit.what: Reverse lookup: the PTR name for an address. Mail servers, logs and some security checks rely on it.
flags: build the in-addr.arpa (or ip6.arpa) query for you

toolkit.what: On systemd-resolved hosts (Ubuntu, Fedora and most desktops), shows which DNS servers and search domains each interface really uses. `/etc/resolv.conf` there only points at 127.0.0.53.
flags: servers and search domains per link
resolve through resolved and say which link answered
toolkit.when: dig and the app disagree, or only the VPN names fail

toolkit.what: Resolves the way most applications do: through `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, so `/etc/hosts` entries and search domains count. dig skips all of that.
flags: IPv4 and IPv6 via the system resolver
every address the resolver library returns

toolkit.what: Windows: dig-like queries with a chosen server and record type. Pair it with `Clear-DnsClientCache` after a change.

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it is for.
pairs: follow the delegation from the root
see what the authoritative server really serves
find the name for an address
resolve the way the application does
see which DNS servers each interface uses

steps.prompt: You moved `api.example.com` to a new IP an hour ago. `dig @ns1.example.com api.example.com +short` shows the new IP; `dig +short api.example.com` on your laptop still shows the old one. The old record had a TTL of 86400. What is happening?
options: Your resolver cached the old answer and may keep it for up to a day; next time lower the TTL well before a move
steps.explain: The authoritative server already serves the new value. Caches keep the old one until its TTL runs out. `dig +noall +answer` against your resolver shows the TTL counting down.

steps.prompt: On a laptop, `dig +short db.corp.internal` returns nothing, but `ping db.corp.internal` works while the VPN is up. Why can they disagree?
options: dig asks only the server listed in `/etc/resolv.conf`, while the system resolver sends `corp.internal` names to the VPN's DNS server (split DNS); check with `resolvectl status` on Linux or `scutil --dns` on macOS
The record has a TTL of 0
steps.explain: Split DNS sends some domains to some servers. Use `resolvectl query` or `getent hosts` to see what apps get, and `dig @<vpn-dns>` to ask the VPN's server directly.

steps.prompt: Show only the answer section, with TTLs, as given by Google's public resolver.
steps.explain: `@` picks the server. `+noall` turns every section off and `+answer` turns the answer back on, so you see name, TTL, type and value. The order matters: `+answer +noall` would hide everything.

steps.prompt: A name resolves to the wrong address for some users. Narrow it down from the source outwards.
lines: dig NS example.com +short   # which servers are authoritative?
dig @ns1.example.com api.example.com +norecurse   # what do they serve?
dig @10.0.0.53 api.example.com +noall +answer   # what does our resolver cache, with what TTL?
getent hosts api.example.com   # what does the app machine actually get?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Lower a record's TTL a day before any planned move, and check the authoritative servers with `+norecurse` right after. When users see different answers, compare authoritative, resolver and `getent` in that order: the first one that differs is where the problem lives.
